question: In April 2022, as part of Scientist Rebellion’s international demonstrations to shine a light on the latest IPCC report, around 100 people took part in a protest outside the Congress of Deputies. They threw a biodegradable red liquid – easily cleaned with water – over the front of the building.
Because of this, 15 people were arrested, and the Madrid Public Prosecutor’s Office is seeking prison sentences of 21 months and a combined fine of EUR 3 300 for damage to property.

Bearing in mind that the Spanish Government approved the Agreement on the Declaration of a Climate and Environmental Emergency in January 2020 and that the climate situation has been deteriorating rapidly in 2023-2024, I would ask the following: 1.
What type of measures is the Commission taking to ensure that the scientific recommendations on the climate emergency are taken into account?
Does the Commission believe that the rights enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union regarding freedom of expression and association are being infringed?
answer: 1. EU climate policy is based on science and informed by the reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Chang e (1). The EU’s goal of climate neutrality and resilience by 2050, which is enshrined in the European Climate Law, along with an interim target of 55% net greenhouse gas reduction by 2030, is science based and consistent with the Paris Agreement longterm temperature goal.
The EU has agreed a package of legislation to meet its commitments and the Commission adopted in February 2024 a communication on a recommended 2040 climate target (2).

To support the achievement of the EU’s climate objectives, the European Climate Law established the European Scientific Advisory Board on Climate Change (3), which provides the EU with scientific knowledge, expertise and independent advice relating to climate change. 2.

Member States must ensure that fundamental rights are effectively respected and protected, in accordance with their national legislation and international human rights obligations. The rights to freedom of expression, of assembly and of association are fundamental rights enshrined in Articles 11 and 12 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU.

The Charter applies to Member States only when they are implementing EU law, in line with its Article 51(1). The definition and application of rules governing the holding of demonstrations, and the sanctions thereof, is a matter which pertains to the Member States only.
